**(1) First message**

```text
gauntlet: question
The framing holds: I checked it against the gather draft only. The draft says the reports page has a table and no export action. It says src/export/csv.ts already reuses the table's column definitions. It names paging as the data path for the 10k-row target. Each of those suggests reuse rather than a new construct. I have not re-read primary code in this session, so these claims remain unverified premises for now, not supported ones.

The draft's premises are that the column definitions and the CSV serializer support export, and that paging supports a 10k-row export in under 60s. I could not trace them to primary code here. They go into `## Problem` as unverified, and the design proceeds on them as stated assumptions.

A verification dependency is also unconfirmed. Row 3 needs a 10k-row report to time against. I have not found a fixture, seed, or test dataset of that size, so that dependency is not checkable from what I have.

The ticket's acceptance criteria include a repo group headed "phase 2", with one row: "Exports are emailed to the requesting user." That heading matches neither this repo (acme/widgets, per the overrides `## Issue tracker`) nor any other known repo. I won't guess where it belongs. Where should that row go?
A) this repo
B) elsewhere: phase 2
C) repair the ticket - /skill:shape-ticket acme/widgets#77
Recommendation: C - "phase 2" reads as a delivery stage rather than a repo, so the ticket is the right place to fix the grouping before this row gets a disposition.
```

---

**(2) Approaches message**

*(Written after the recorded answers: the button goes beside the report title, and the export uses the visible table columns in table order. The "phase 2" question has no recorded answer. Its row stays undispositioned and is carried to Open Questions. The approaches below cover the three acme/widgets rows and design no email delivery.)*

Two dependencies still stand open. First, the 10k-row dataset for row 3. I looked for it in the gather draft's account and found no fixture or seed of that size, so it is not checkable yet. The spec will need one created, or an existing large report named, before the timing can be observed. Second, I could not confirm whether csv.ts honours column visibility and order. The draft says it reuses the column definitions but not whether it filters to visible ones. If it doesn't, that becomes a change to csv.ts rather than a new serializer.

I recommend **A: client-side export through the existing serializer**. The axis separating the options is where the export runs.

**A) Client-side export through the existing serializer (reuse-only).** A new Export CSV button sits beside the report title. On click, it pulls all rows through the existing paging. It serializes them with src/export/csv.ts, passing the table's visible column definitions in table order, and triggers a download. Nothing new sits in the data path; the serializer and paging are used as they already exist.

The trade-off is that 10k rows are paged into the browser. That relies on the draft's claim that paging meets the 60s target, which is unverified. Memory use on large reports is the risk. If csv.ts lacks visible-column filtering, that becomes a parameter on csv.ts. csv.ts has other callers, so the parameter must default to today's behaviour.

Removes: none
Adds: Export CSV button beside the report title on the reports page; click handler that pages all rows and calls csv.ts with visible columns in table order; a visible-columns parameter on csv.ts if absent; tests for the button, column set and order, and the 10k-row timing
Pattern: follows src/export/csv.ts's reuse of the table's column definitions, with no second column list and no parallel serializer.

**B) Server-side export endpoint (drops the assumption that export happens in the browser).** The button calls a new endpoint. The endpoint reads the report through the same paging, streams CSV rows via csv.ts, and returns a file download. This moves the 10k-row load off the client and makes the timing independent of browser memory.

The cost is a new route, auth on it, and passing the visible-column selection from the client to the server. That selection is UI state the server doesn't own today.

Removes: none
Adds: export endpoint/route; server-side handler calling paging and csv.ts; request parameter carrying visible columns and their order; the Export CSV button beside the report title; endpoint, column, and 10k-row timing tests
Pattern: reuses src/export/csv.ts, but adds a new boundary and splits column-visibility state across client and server, which cuts against the table owning its column definitions.

A follows the existing pattern with the fewest moving parts. I would switch to B if timing a 10k-row client-side export shows it misses 60s, or if browser memory fails on it.
